e.meaning: short for Jackson, son of Jack
e.etymology: A respelling of Jax, a modern short form of Jackson, the surname meaning son of Jack.
A Hebrew name meaning the Lord has answered, borne by a man who stands beside Ezra in the Book of Nehemiah. American parents now give it mostly to girls, where it also reads as a spelling of Anaya.
A modern American coinage, close kin to Ayanna and Ayana. Baby-name books often call it Native American for eternal blossom, but no source in a tribal language has been shown.
From Greek Zephyros, the god of the west wind, the gentlest of the winds and the bringer of spring. In English a zephyr is a soft, mild breeze.
A modern Turkish girls' name. Alara is also the name of a river and a medieval castle on Turkey's Mediterranean coast; its original meaning is not settled.
The Ashkenazi pronunciation of Hebrew Yitzchak, the original of Isaac, from the verb for laughing. In Genesis, Sarah laughs when told she will bear a son in old age, and the child is named for it.
In the US, a recent name in the style of Amari, Kamari and Makai. Makari is also an Eastern Christian form of Macarius, from Greek makarios (blessed), the name of several early saints.
A back-formation from Darlene, an American name built on the word darling. It took off in the mid-20th century, helped by Darla Hood of the Our Gang comedies.
namesakes: Darla Hood (child star of Our Gang, The Little Rascals)
Darla (the fish-tapping niece in Finding Nemo)

assoc.t: Darla, Alfalfa's sweetheart in The Little Rascals

e.etymology: The Hebrew original of Simon and Simeon, traditionally derived from shama (to hear). In Genesis, Shimon is the second son of Jacob and Leah and the founder of one of the twelve tribes.
namesakes: Shimon Peres (Israeli prime minister, president and Nobel Peace laureate)

e.etymology: From the surname of a powerful Scottish clan, taken from a place in Berwickshire whose name may be Brythonic for spacious fort. It became a first name in the 19th century, partly in honor of General Charles Gordon.
namesakes: Gordon Ramsay (chef and host of Hell's Kitchen)
Gordon Lightfoot (Canadian folk singer)
Gordon Gekko (greed-is-good financier in Wall Street)

assoc.t: Gordon Ramsay, celebrity chef
Commissioner Gordon, Batman's police ally
Gordon's, London dry gin

e.etymology: The English form of French Henriette, the feminine of Henri (Henry), from Germanic words for home and ruler. It was popular in England and America in the 18th and 19th centuries.
namesakes: Harriet Tubman (abolitionist and Underground Railroad conductor)
Harriet Beecher Stowe (author of Uncle Tom's Cabin)
Harriet M. Welsch (the young sleuth of Harriet the Spy)

assoc.t: Harriet Tubman, Underground Railroad conductor
Harriet the Spy, heroine of the classic children's novel

e.etymology: Invented by Sir Walter Scott for a Saxon noble in Ivanhoe (1819), apparently by altering Cerdic, the name of an early king of Wessex, which may be of Welsh origin. Little Lord Fauntleroy later spread it.
namesakes: Cedric the Entertainer (comedian and actor)
Cedric Diggory (Hufflepuff champion in Harry Potter)
Cedric Errol (the boy hero of Little Lord Fauntleroy)

assoc.t: Cedric the Entertainer, comedian and actor
Cedric Diggory, Hufflepuff champion in Harry Potter

e.etymology: From the Italian surname D'Angelo (of Angelo), from Greek angelos (messenger, angel). It became an African American given name in the 1990s, usually written D'Angelo or DeAngelo.
namesakes: D'Angelo (neo-soul singer of Brown Sugar)
D'Angelo Russell (NBA guard)
D'Angelo Barksdale (character on The Wire)

assoc.t: D'Angelo, the neo-soul singer

e.etymology: A respelling of Collins, an English surname meaning son of Colin, a medieval pet form of Nicholas, and also an Irish surname from O Coileain. Collins became a girls' name in the 2010s.

e.meaning: pet form of William, resolute protector
e.etymology: A pet form of William by way of Bill. William comes from Germanic words for will and helmet, and Billy has long been given as a name in its own right, especially in the American South.
namesakes: Billy Joel (Piano Man singer-songwriter)
Billy Graham (evangelist)
Billy the Kid (Old West outlaw)

assoc.t: Billy the Kid, Wild West outlaw
billy goat, a male goat

e.etymology: An African American coinage that adds the prefix De-, as in DeShawn and DeAngelo, to Andre, the French form of Andrew, from Greek andreios (manly). It is often written DeAndre.
namesakes: DeAndre Hopkins (NFL wide receiver)
DeAndre Jordan (NBA center)
Deandre Ayton (NBA center)

e.etymology: From Arabic yusra, from the root for ease, comfort and good fortune. The word appears in the Quran, in a verse promising that the path will be made easy.
The feminine of Ivan, the Slavic form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan (God is gracious). It is common in Czech, Slovak and South Slavic countries and is also used in Latin America.
namesakes: Ivana Trump (businesswoman, first wife of Donald Trump)

assoc.t: Ivana Trump, first wife of Donald Trump

e.note: Sounds like I wanna, the setup for joke names such as Ivana Humpalot in Austin Powers.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Kena'an, the land promised to Abraham's descendants and also the name of a grandson of Noah. The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain.

assoc.t: Canaan, the Promised Land of the Bible

e.etymology: From the old Germanic word karl (free man), the same root as Charles, which reached English through German and Scandinavian Carl and Karl. It is the name of many Swedish kings, including Carl XVI Gustaf.
namesakes: Carl Sagan (astronomer and host of Cosmos)
Carl Jung (founder of analytical psychology)
Carl Fredricksen (the balloon-flying widower in Pixar's Up)

assoc.t: Carl's Jr., fast food burger chain

e.etymology: From an English surname taken from the Yorkshire town of Beverley, Old English befer (beaver) plus leah (clearing). Once a man's name, it turned feminine after the 1904 novel Beverly of Graustark and the fame of Beverly Hills.
namesakes: Beverly Cleary (author of the Ramona children's books)
Beverly Crusher (Star Trek: The Next Generation doctor)
Beverly Sills (opera soprano)

assoc.t: Beverly Hills, the wealthy Los Angeles-area city

e.etymology: A pet form of Elizabeth, and sometimes of Isabel, now often given as a name in its own right. Elizabeth comes from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. In modern Hebrew, Libi also reads as my heart.

assoc.t: Libby's canned pumpkin, vegetables and fruit
Libby, the library ebook and audiobook app

e.etymology: The German, Polish and Czech spelling of Dominic, from Late Latin Dominicus, of the Lord, from dominus (lord). Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican order, spread the name across Catholic Europe.
namesakes: Dominik Hasek (Hall of Fame hockey goaltender)
Dominik Mysterio (WWE wrestler)

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Kinley, a surname shortened from McKinley. McKinley is the Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaigh, son of Fionnlagh, a name built from fionn (fair) and laoch (warrior).
A recent elaboration with no history of its own, most likely Ana joined to Leia or Leah, in the same family as Analia and Annalee.

From an English surname that goes back to the Old Norse name Havardr, from har (high) and vardr (guard). Its use as a first name spread in the 19th century, helped by the prestige of the noble Howard family.
namesakes: Howard Hughes (aviator and film tycoon)
Howard Stern (radio host)
Howard Wolowitz (The Big Bang Theory engineer)

assoc.t: Howard University, historically Black university in DC
Howard Stern, radio host
Howard the Duck, Marvel comics character

e.etymology: The Russian form of Leo, from the Slavic word lev (lion). In Hebrew lev means heart, and Jewish families also use the name in that sense.
namesakes: Lev Tolstoy (Russian novelist known in English as Leo Tolstoy)

e.etymology: A respelling of Crew, the English word for a team that works together, which came into use as a boys' name in the 2010s.
A respelling of Briar, the English word for a thorny wild shrub such as the wild rose. Bryer is also an English surname.

The English form of Susanna, from Hebrew Shoshannah (lily), a word that goes back to the Egyptian name for the lotus flower. It was one of the most popular girls' names in America in the 1950s and 1960s.
namesakes: Susan B. Anthony (women's suffrage leader)
Susan Sarandon (Oscar-winning actress)
Susan Pevensie (The Chronicles of Narnia sibling)

assoc.t: lazy Susan, the rotating serving tray
black-eyed Susan, the yellow wildflower

e.etymology: The English word essence, from Latin essentia (being). It came into use as a girls' name in the United States in the late 20th century, mainly in African American families.

assoc.t: Essence, the magazine for Black women
Essence Festival, annual music festival in New Orleans
essence, drugstore makeup brand

e.etymology: Feminine of the Roman name Tatianus, from Tatius, a family name of obscure origin. Saint Tatiana made it a favorite in the Orthodox Church, and English took it from Russian.
namesakes: Tatiana Maslany (Orphan Black actress)
Grand Duchess Tatiana (daughter of Russia's last tsar)
